subtopic_detail: Creatinine 212 after three days of vomiting in a man taking a diuretic, a blocker of the renin system and ibuprofen
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 74 year old retired fitter who has had three days of vomiting and watery diarrhoea since a family barbecue. He has kept almost nothing down and feels faint when he stands.

His regular medications are perindopril, indapamide, empagliflozin, metformin and atorvastatin, and he has been buying ibuprofen for his knee for the past month. He has taken all of them every day through the illness because, as he puts it, he was told never to miss a dose. He has passed only a small amount of dark urine since yesterday. He has no abdominal pain, no urinary symptoms and no history of prostatic obstruction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/64 mmHg standing from 150/80 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not visible, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 212 micromol/L (60-110) from a baseline of 92, potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 18.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 9.2 mmol/L, blood ketones 0.6 mmol/L (less than 0.6), urinalysis negative for blood and protein, bladder scan shows 20 mL

lead_in: Alongside intravenous rehydration, which of his medications should be withheld today?

options.text: Perindopril, indapamide, ibuprofen, metformin and empagliflozin
options.rationale: The diuretic, the blocker of the renin angiotensin system and the anti-inflammatory are the three drugs that together convert a simple volume loss into acute kidney injury, and all three are withheld. Metformin is withheld because it accumulates and risks lactic acidosis at this level of function, and the sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor because it drives osmotic diuresis and ketogenesis during illness, which is why sick day advice covers five drugs here rather than three. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.text: Perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen, continuing the other three
options.rationale: Stopping the three drugs responsible for the haemodynamic injury is the core of the answer and is what most clinicians remember, but continuing metformin at an estimated filtration rate in the twenties risks lactic acidosis, and continuing the glucose lowering agent that acts on the kidney tubule prolongs the fluid losses. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.text: Metformin and empagliflozin only, continuing the other four
options.rationale: Withholding the diabetes medications addresses the metabolic risks and leaves the cause of the injury running, since the combination of a diuretic, a blocker of the renin angiotensin system and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory is what removes the kidney's ability to defend its filtration pressure during volume depletion. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.text: Ibuprofen only, continuing his five other regular medications
options.rationale: The anti-inflammatory is the most obviously avoidable of the group and the one he chose himself, but removing it alone leaves efferent arteriolar dilatation from the renin blocker and ongoing sodium loss from the thiazide like diuretic in a man who is already volume depleted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: All six of his regular medications including the atorvastatin
options.rationale: The statin is neither nephrotoxic nor cleared in a way that matters here, and reflexively stopping everything is how patients end up never restarting drugs with prognostic benefit. Sick day rules name specific classes rather than suspending the whole list. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

explanation.summary: The combination of a diuretic, an inhibitor of the renin angiotensin system and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is known as the triple whammy and roughly triples the risk of acute kidney injury, because the diuretic depletes volume, the anti-inflammatory removes the prostaglandin mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation that preserves glomerular perfusion, and the renin blocker removes the angiotensin mediated efferent constriction that preserves filtration pressure. Any acute volume loss on top of that, typically gastroenteritis in an older person, produces exactly this picture. Sick day management plans are issued in Australian practice to patients on these drugs and instruct them to withhold specified medications during any illness with vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or sweats, and to restart when eating and drinking normally for twenty four to forty eight hours. The classes covered are the renin angiotensin blockers, diuretics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, metformin and sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. The latter deserve particular attention because they can precipitate ketoacidosis with only modestly raised glucose during illness, so ketones are measured rather than relying on the glucose reading.
key_points: Diuretic plus renin blocker plus anti-inflammatory is the triple whammy of acute kidney injury
Anti-inflammatories remove afferent dilatation and renin blockers remove efferent constriction
Sick day rules also cover metformin and sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors
Restart withheld drugs after twenty four to forty eight hours of normal intake
Statins and most other regular medicines are continued rather than suspended
explanation.pearls: Measure blood ketones rather than glucose in any unwell patient taking a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, because ketoacidosis on these drugs typically occurs with a glucose below 14 mmol/L and is missed entirely if the glucose reading is used as the screening test.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

subtopic_detail: Blood pressure 232/128 with flash pulmonary oedema and a plan to bring the pressure to normal within the hour
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to a 58 year old delivery driver who became severely breathless two hours ago and cannot lie flat. He is sitting bolt upright, speaking in single words, and coughing up frothy pink sputum.

He ran out of his blood pressure tablets three weeks ago and has not been back to his general practitioner. He has no chest pain, no tearing interscapular pain, no headache and no visual disturbance, and his radial and femoral pulses are symmetrical. The intern has drawn up a large dose of frusemide and asks whether the aim is to get the blood pressure back to normal before the next set of observations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 232/128 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute, SpO2 86 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward and using accessory muscles, sweating, crackles to both mid zones, third heart sound, no murmur, calves soft, no focal neurological signs, fundi show flame haemorrhages without papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and lateral repolarisation change and no ST elevation, high sensitivity troponin 45 ng/L (less than 16), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar alveolar shadowing with a normal mediastinal contour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide alone and aim for normal blood pressure within the hour
options.rationale: These patients are usually not volume overloaded but have redistributed fluid into the lungs under an enormous afterload, so large diuretic doses can worsen intravascular depletion and raise creatinine while doing little for the mechanism. Diuretic is an adjunct, given in modest dose, not the primary treatment. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Give intravenous metoprolol and aim to reduce the mean pressure by a quarter
options.rationale: The pressure target is right but the agent is wrong: intravenous beta blockade in acute pulmonary oedema removes the sympathetic support the failing ventricle is relying on and can precipitate cardiogenic shock. Beta blockade belongs in aortic dissection and after the acute decompensation has resolved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion and aim to reduce the mean pressure by a quarter
options.rationale: Severe hypertension with acute pulmonary oedema is driven by afterload, and a titratable nitrate infusion reduces preload at low dose and afterload as it is increased, relieving the oedema within minutes, alongside high flow oxygen and non-invasive ventilation. The reduction is limited to about twenty to twenty five per cent of the mean arterial pressure in the first hour because a chronically hypertensive brain and kidney have shifted their autoregulation and cannot tolerate a rapid fall. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Give sublingual nifedipine and aim for normal blood pressure within the first hour
options.rationale: Short acting sublingual calcium channel blockade produces an uncontrolled and unpredictable fall in pressure and has caused strokes and myocardial infarction, which is why it was abandoned. It combines the wrong route with the wrong target. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Start an oral antihypertensive and aim for normal blood pressure over twenty four hours
options.rationale: Gradual oral reduction over a day is exactly right for severe hypertension without organ damage, which is urgency rather than emergency, but he has acute pulmonary oedema and a rising troponin, so there is organ damage happening now and an oral agent cannot be titrated against it. The distinction between the two situations is the presence of acute end organ injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension accompanied by acute end organ injury, and the organ involved dictates both the drug and the target. Acute pulmonary oedema, encephalopathy, aortic dissection, eclampsia, acute coronary syndrome and acute kidney injury are the usual syndromes, and without any of them the situation is hypertensive urgency, managed with oral agents over twenty four to forty eight hours and outpatient follow up. In pulmonary oedema the mechanism is afterload mismatch rather than fluid excess, so a titratable nitrate infusion is the primary agent, combined with high flow oxygen and non-invasive ventilation, and diuretic in modest dose only if there is genuine volume overload. The general target is a reduction of no more than twenty to twenty five per cent in the mean arterial pressure in the first hour, then to around 160 over 100 mmHg over the next several hours, because chronic hypertension shifts cerebral autoregulation rightwards and an abrupt normalisation can cause watershed infarction and blindness. The two exceptions that require faster and deeper reduction are aortic dissection, where the systolic target is under 120 mmHg within twenty minutes with beta blockade first, and eclampsia.
key_points: Emergency requires acute end organ injury; without it the situation is urgency
Pulmonary oedema here is an afterload problem rather than volume overload
A titratable nitrate infusion with oxygen and non-invasive ventilation is first line
Limit the fall to twenty to twenty five per cent of mean pressure in the first hour
Aortic dissection and eclampsia are the exceptions requiring faster reduction
explanation.pearls: Flame haemorrhages without papilloedema place this at grade 3 retinopathy, which tells you the hypertension is severe and accelerated but has not yet produced raised intracranial pressure, and a bedside fundoscopy in a patient who cannot give a history is often the fastest way to establish that the blood pressure is chronic rather than an acute pain response.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Sudden urge with leakage on the way to the toilet and three voids a night in a woman of sixty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old retired teacher with twelve months of a sudden desperate need to pass urine, with leakage before she reaches the toilet about three times a week. She gets up three times a night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes, laughs or lifts her grandchildren, and she has no sensation of anything coming down. She had two vaginal births in her thirties. She drinks six cups of tea and two cans of diet cola a day and takes no diuretic. Her last period was eleven years ago and she uses no hormone therapy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, pale thin vaginal epithelium with loss of rugae, no descent of the anterior or posterior wall beyond the hymen on straining, no leak demonstrated on cough, voluntary pelvic floor contraction present but weak
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes, blood and glucose, post void residual volume 30 mL on bladder scan, glycated haemoglobin 38 mmol/mol, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies before starting any treatment for these symptoms
options.rationale: Urodynamic testing is reserved for symptoms that fail conservative treatment, for mixed or unclear patterns, and before surgery for stress incontinence, because in a clear storage pattern with a negative dipstick and a normal residual it does not change the first line plan. It also carries cost, discomfort and a risk of infection. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic treatment is second line after behavioural measures, and oxybutynin in particular is the agent most associated with dry mouth, constipation and cognitive impairment in older women, with accumulating evidence linking long term anticholinergic load to dementia. If a drug is needed later, a more selective agent or a beta 3 agonist is preferred. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Refer for a midurethral sling procedure and review her six weeks afterwards
options.rationale: A sling treats leakage on effort by supporting the urethra, and she has none: no leak on coughing, sneezing or lifting, and none demonstrable on examination. Operating on the wrong mechanism can worsen urgency and cause voiding difficulty. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start mirabegron 25 mg daily and review her symptoms in three months time
options.rationale: A beta 3 agonist avoids the anticholinergic burden and is a good second line choice in this age group, but drug treatment still follows a proper trial of behavioural measures because roughly half of women improve substantially without any medication. Blood pressure also needs monitoring on this agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology

options.text: Start bladder training with caffeine reduction and pelvic floor exercises
options.rationale: Urgency with urge leakage and nocturia, with no stress component, no prolapse, a negative dipstick and a normal residual, is an overactive bladder, and first line treatment is behavioural: a bladder diary, timed voiding with progressively lengthened intervals, reduction of caffeine and of evening fluids, weight loss, and supervised pelvic floor muscle training which suppresses detrusor contractions as well as supporting the urethra. Eight cups of caffeinated drinks a day is a directly modifiable contributor. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence in women is separated first into stress, urgency and mixed patterns, because the treatments diverge completely: stress incontinence responds to pelvic floor training and, if that fails, to a continence procedure, while urgency incontinence responds to bladder retraining and then to drug treatment. The initial assessment needs only a history, a bladder diary, an examination for prolapse and pelvic floor function, a urine dipstick to exclude infection, haematuria and glycosuria, and a post void residual. Behavioural treatment achieves substantial improvement in around half of women with an overactive bladder and carries no adverse effects, so it precedes any prescription. When drug treatment is needed, antimuscarinics and beta 3 agonists are roughly equivalent in efficacy, and the choice turns on adverse effects, with anticholinergic load a genuine concern in older women. Vaginal oestrogen is a useful adjunct where there is urogenital atrophy, and refractory cases proceed to specialist options including intravesical botulinum toxin and sacral neuromodulation.
key_points: Separate stress from urgency first because the treatments diverge completely
Dipstick, bladder diary, prolapse assessment and post void residual are the initial workup
Behavioural treatment helps around half of women and precedes any drug
Oxybutynin carries the highest anticholinergic burden and is a poor choice in older women
Urodynamics is for treatment failure, unclear patterns or before continence surgery
explanation.pearls: Topical vaginal oestrogen is worth adding here alongside the bladder training: atrophic changes of the urethra and trigone contribute to urgency and frequency after menopause, and low dose vaginal preparations produce negligible systemic absorption, so they are usable even in women for whom systemic hormone therapy is not appropriate.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: Coarse facial and chest hair developing gradually over two years with testosterone 3.2 at twenty four
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old retail manager who has been shaving her chin and upper lip daily for the past year and has noticed coarse dark hairs appearing between her breasts. The change has come on gradually over about two years.

Her periods come every forty to sixty days and have done so since she was sixteen. Her voice has not changed, she has no increase in muscle bulk and she has not noticed any change in her external genitalia or thinning at her temples. She is not trying to conceive, uses condoms, and has no personal or family history of migraine, thrombosis or breast cancer. She does not smoke.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, coarse terminal hair over the chin, upper lip, periareolar area and linea alba, no clitoromegaly, no temporal recession, no abdominal or pelvic mass, no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 3.2 nmol/L (0.3-1.8), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate within normal limits, early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone within normal limits, prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), pelvic ultrasound shows multifollicular ovaries with normal volume and no adnexal mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for the hair growth?

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and review her hair growth in six months
options.rationale: Metformin improves insulin resistance, menstrual regularity and ovulation in this condition and has a place, but its effect on hair growth is minimal and it is not recommended as treatment for hirsutism. It would be the right choice if the target were cycle regulation or metabolic risk. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Start spironolactone 100 mg daily and review her hair growth in six months
options.rationale: Androgen receptor blockade is effective and is added after six months if the first line treatment has not achieved enough, but used alone in a woman of reproductive age it requires reliable contraception because of the risk of undervirilisation of a male foetus. The sequence, not the drug, is what is wrong here. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Refer for computed tomography of the adrenal glands and pelvic ultrasound
options.rationale: Imaging for an androgen secreting tumour is warranted with rapid onset over months, virilisation such as clitoromegaly, deepening voice or temporal balding, or a testosterone above about 5 nmol/L, and none of those apply to a gradual two year history with a modest elevation. Her pelvic ultrasound has already been done and shows no mass. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive and review the hair at six months
options.rationale: Gradual hirsutism with oligomenorrhoea since adolescence, a modestly raised testosterone, normal adrenal androgens and normal 17 hydroxyprogesterone is polycystic ovary syndrome, and combined hormonal contraception is first line for the hair because it suppresses ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone binding globulin. Six months is the minimum interval for assessing response because the hair growth cycle takes that long to turn over. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.text: Start finasteride 5 mg daily and review her hair growth in six months time
options.rationale: Five alpha reductase inhibitors have some efficacy for hirsutism but are not approved for this use in women, carry the same teratogenic risk to a male foetus as other antiandrogens, and are not recommended ahead of the established options. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Hirsutism means coarse terminal hair in an androgen dependent distribution and is quantified with the modified Ferriman Gallwey score, with a threshold around four to six in most populations. The critical triage is between the common causes, overwhelmingly polycystic ovary syndrome and idiopathic hirsutism, and the rare serious ones: an androgen secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour, non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia and Cushing syndrome. Red flags for a tumour are rapid progression over months rather than years, frank virilisation with clitoromegaly, deepening of the voice or temporal balding, onset well after adolescence, and a total testosterone above roughly 5 nmol/L or twice the upper limit of normal. Non-classical adrenal hyperplasia is screened for with an early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase. Treatment of the hair itself is combined hormonal contraception first, with an antiandrogen added after six months if the response is insufficient, alongside mechanical or laser hair removal, and any assessment of response requires at least six months because of the length of the hair growth cycle.
key_points: Rapid onset, virilisation or testosterone above about 5 nmol/L suggests a tumour
Early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone screens for non-classical adrenal hyperplasia
Combined hormonal contraception is first line for hirsutism in polycystic ovary syndrome
Antiandrogens are added after six months and require reliable contraception
Assess response no earlier than six months because of the hair growth cycle
explanation.pearls: Warn her that the contraceptive will stop new terminal hairs developing but will not remove the ones already there, since existing terminal hair does not revert to fine vellus hair, which is why laser or electrolysis is offered alongside rather than after the hormonal treatment and why unrealistic expectations are the usual reason women abandon it at three months.

sources.label: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic positive chlamydia nucleic acid test on routine antenatal screening at twelve weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 24 year old woman in her first pregnancy at twelve weeks and two days. Her booking investigations included a self collected vaginal swab, which has returned positive for Chlamydia trachomatis on nucleic acid amplification testing.

She has no discharge, no pelvic pain, no bleeding and no urinary symptoms. Testing for gonorrhoea on the same swab was negative, and her syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B serology were all non-reactive. She has had one regular partner for eighteen months and reports no other partners in that time. She has no drug allergies and is taking only pregnancy multivitamins.

data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, abdomen non-tender, no cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab nucleic acid amplification test positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B serology non-reactive, haemoglobin 122 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), midstream urine shows no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days with a test of cure in four weeks
options.rationale: A seven day tetracycline course is the preferred regimen outside pregnancy because it has higher cure rates, particularly for rectal infection, but tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy because of deposition in developing teeth and bone. The duration is not the issue; the class is. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose with a test of cure in four weeks
options.rationale: A single dose macrolide is the recommended treatment for genital chlamydia in pregnancy, being effective and safe in all trimesters, and a test of cure is performed at four weeks specifically because pregnancy is one of the situations where confirming eradication matters, given the risks of preterm birth and of neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia. Her partner is treated at the same time to prevent reinfection. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for seven days with no test of cure
options.rationale: Amoxicillin is a recognised alternative in pregnancy when a macrolide cannot be used, but it has lower microbiological cure rates and there is concern about driving latent infection, so it is second line rather than the default. Omitting the test of cure compounds the problem. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.text: Defer treatment until after delivery and repeat the swab in the third trimester
options.rationale: Untreated infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth, premature rupture of membranes and low birth weight, and with neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia acquired during vaginal birth, so deferral exposes both mother and baby to preventable harm. Asymptomatic infection is treated exactly as symptomatic infection is. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once with a test of cure in four weeks time
options.rationale: A cephalosporin injection is the treatment for gonorrhoea, which her swab specifically excluded, and it has no useful activity against this intracellular organism. The pairing of the two infections in practice makes this an easy substitution to make by reflex. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

explanation.summary: Chlamydia is the most frequently notified sexually transmitted infection in Australia, with the highest rates in people aged fifteen to twenty nine, and it is asymptomatic in about three quarters of infected women, which is why antenatal screening and annual screening of sexually active people under thirty are both recommended. Treatment differs by setting: outside pregnancy the preferred regimen is doxycycline for seven days, reflecting evidence of superior cure rates particularly at rectal sites, while in pregnancy a single dose of azithromycin is used because tetracyclines are contraindicated. A test of cure is not routine for uncomplicated genital infection but is recommended in pregnancy, after rectal infection, where adherence is uncertain and where an alternative regimen was used, and it is performed at four weeks because nucleic acid tests detect residual non-viable organism before then. Partner notification covering sexual contacts from the preceding six months is an integral part of management, and retesting for reinfection at three months is advised because reinfection from an untreated partner is common. Untreated maternal infection risks preterm birth and neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia.
key_points: Around three quarters of infections in women are asymptomatic, hence routine screening
Doxycycline for seven days outside pregnancy; single dose azithromycin in pregnancy
Test of cure at four weeks is recommended in pregnancy, not routinely otherwise
Partner notification covers contacts from the preceding six months
Retest for reinfection at three months regardless of the initial cure
explanation.pearls: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis presents between five and fourteen days after birth, later than the gonococcal form which appears in the first two to five days, and it is treated with oral rather than topical erythromycin because the organism also colonises the nasopharynx and can cause an afebrile pneumonia at four to twelve weeks of age.

sources.label: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
